issues.item: Escape Route Planning: always plan an escape route before entering a place
issues.explanation: Escape route planning implies a prominent ongoing external-danger/triggered-threat pattern in public places, but the formulation specifies no active links involving Triggers or Threat, and the rest of the profile is centered on bodily vulnerability and negative beliefs rather than situational danger. This makes the item poorly aligned with the formulation and cross-node content.

issues.item: Distrust Others: People are not what they seem
issues.explanation: Distrust of others is not impossible after a life-threatening accident, but in this profile it introduces an interpersonal/paranoid theme that is not supported by the other selected items or the formulation. The remaining items focus on bodily unreliability and permanent damage after an accident, so this item is the least coherent with the trauma-linked appraisal pattern presented.

vignette:
Rashid is a 75-year-old widowed sculptor of Middle Eastern descent, a man who has spent decades coaxing form from stone, trusting his hands and his body to translate vision into mass. That trust shattered eighteen months ago, when a chain hoist in his studio gave way and a half-finished block of granite, weighing nearly four hundred pounds, swung free and pinned him against the wall. He remembers the sound of his own ribs cracking, the impossible pressure against his chest, the certainty that he was being crushed from the inside out. He lay pinned for twenty-two minutes before a neighbor heard his shouts. In the hospital, they told him he was lucky—three fractured ribs, a collapsed lung, no spinal damage. But Rashid did not feel lucky. He felt, for the first time in his life, that his body had betrayed him.

In the months that followed, that feeling calcified into something harder. Rashid came to believe that his body was no longer something he could rely on—that it had become fragile, unpredictable, a vessel that could break without warning. He became convinced that the accident had permanently damaged him, not just in the ribs that still ached in cold weather, but in some deeper, irreversible way. He would catch himself staring at his hands, those hands that had once shaped mountains of marble, and think: I am not the same man. I will never be the same man. This belief was not a passing thought; it became the lens through which he saw everything. He began to monitor his body constantly—checking his pulse when he stood up, pressing on his ribs to see if they still hurt, scanning for any twinge or ache that might signal another catastrophe. What frightened him most was the possibility that his body would simply give out again, that he would be caught off guard. He had come to believe that the only way to stay safe was to stay vigilant.

This vigilance soon shaped his days. Rashid stopped working with heavy stone altogether; he could not bear the thought of standing beneath a hoist or lifting anything that might strain his chest. He told himself it was temporary, that he would return to the studio when he felt stronger, but he never did. Instead, he found himself avoiding any situation that put his body under stress—no more morning walks to the market, no more carrying groceries, no more climbing the ladder to clean the gutters. He began to think constantly about why the accident had happened to him, turning it over in his mind like a stone he could not set down. Was it punishment? Carelessness? Some failing he could not name? He would lie awake at three in the morning, replaying the moment the hoist gave way, searching for a meaning that never arrived.

The causal loop tightened: the more he appraised his body as damaged and untrustworthy, the more he felt compelled to monitor and shield it. And the more he monitored and avoided, the more his body atrophied—his muscles softened, his back ached from disuse, his breath grew shallow—which only confirmed his belief that he was permanently broken. He withdrew from his adult children, who lived in another state, because he did not want them to see him diminished. He stopped attending the weekly sculpture critique group he had hosted for thirty years; the thought of explaining why he no longer worked felt unbearable. His studio gathered dust. His hands, once so sure, now trembled slightly when he tried to hold a chisel.

What finally brought Rashid to seek help was not his own suffering, but a quiet moment with his granddaughter during a rare visit. She asked him, without judgment, why he no longer made anything. He could not answer her. That night, he called his doctor and asked for a referral. He is terrified that therapy will force him to confront the accident again, and he is equally terrified that without it, he will spend whatever years he has left watching himself shrink into a man he no longer recognizes.
